stories.headline: Iran president meets PM Modi, seeks help to end war
stories.title: Iran president meets PM Modi, seeks help to end war
stories.summary: Prime Minister Modi convened with Iranian President Pezeshkian to advance discussions on fortifying trade connections between their nations. Both leaders acknowledged the critical role of maritime freedom and trade in the region. They also discussed the ongoing situations in West Asia, focusing on the importance of Chabahar port collaboration. President Pezeshkian encouraged India to mediate for peace, underscoring their shared dedication to enhancing bilateral economic cooperation.

stories.headline: Rethinking Himalayan Floods
stories.title: Rethinking Himalayan Floods
stories.summary: The flash floods that tore through the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 were, for a few days, were described as a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF). That assumption turned out to be wrong. Satellite analysis later showed the disaster began not with a lake bursting its banks, but with a chunk of glacier, ice and rock giving way on an unstable slope and crashing into a river valley below. For years, the dominant framework for understanding Himalayan flood risk has been the glacial lake. The Nepal event is a reminder that a slope does not need a lake beneath it to become a disaster. Fractured bedrock and glacier ice sitting on a steep incline can fail on their own, and once that debris reaches a river channel, it can turn into a flood just as destructive as a GLOF. Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh have already been flagged as the most climate-sensitive part of the Himalayan range, warming faster than other sectors and facing much sharper temperature rises in the decades ahead. Kishtwar, Doda, Ramban and large parts of Ladakh sit in terrain that scientists say closely resembles the slopes that failed in Nepal. Kashmir’s own glacial lake studies have already flagged thousands of buildings and more than a dozen bridges within potential flood zones. What has not been done, by the scientists’ own account, is a comparable assessment of the unstable rock and ice slopes themselves. A disaster elsewhere prompts a round of statements and studies, some monitoring stations go up, and attention moves on before the harder work of mapping is finished. Permafrost and bedrock studies are slower and less visible, and there is no local memory of a slope collapse in the way there is of a lake breach. That should not be mistaken for safety. The scientists quoted after the Nepal disaster are asking for something more basic: that the slopes above Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh be studied with the same seriousness as the lakes below them, before one of them fails without warning. Given how much of the region’s population and infrastructure sits downstream, that is a reasonable ask, and one the government should not wait for the next disaster to act on.

stories.headline: Army reviews operational preparedness along LoC
stories.title: Army reviews operational preparedness along LoC
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 31: General Officer Commanding (GOC) White Knight Corps, Lieutenant General P K Mishra visited the Ace of Spades Division to review its operational preparedness and assess the evolving security dynamics, the Army said on Monday. During the visit, the Corps Commander was briefed on the division’s operational commitments, capability development, Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) and counter-UAS capabilities, besides the roadmap for enhancing operational effectiveness in the coming days. The Army said the visit focused on strengthening preparedness in view of the changing battlefield environment and emerging security challenges. The Corps Commander emphasised the need to further enhance operational effectiveness and exhorted all ranks to remain future-ready, agile and adaptable to emerging challenges. The White Knight Corps, which is responsible for the security of the Jammu region including areas along the Line of Control (LoC) has been regularly reviewing operational preparedness and surveillance capabilities amid evolving security dynamics. In a post on X, the White Knight Corps said: “GOC White Knight Corps visited Ace of Spades Division to review operational preparedness and assess the evolving security dynamics. He was briefed on operational commitments, capability development, UAS & Counter-UAS capabilities and the roadmap ahead.” The Army further said the Corps Commander emphasised enhancing operational effectiveness in an evolving battlefield environment and exhorted all ranks to remain “Future Ready, agile and adaptable” to emerging challenges. The Ace of Spades Division headquartered in the Rajouri-Poonch region is responsible for operational preparedness in a strategically important area along the LoC.

stories.headline: The Mehdi–Abdullah Rupture
stories.title: The Mehdi–Abdullah Rupture
stories.summary: There is a particular cruelty in watching a political marriage end in public, especially when both parties insist the other has broken faith with something larger than themselves. That is the spectacle Jammu and Kashmir has been offered this August, as Srinagar’s Lok Sabha member Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi and National Conference president Dr Farooq Abdullah traded accusations that go well beyond personal pique. Mehdi has now announced he will resign his seat on 3 November, the anniversary of his father’s assassination. Abdullah, for his part, has told him to go and test his standing with the electorate, warning him darkly to remember what happened to the “14 people” who once conspired against his own government in 1984. Beneath the theatre lies a genuine and consequential argument about what the National Conference’s 2024 mandate actually meant, and about whether a party can keep its soul while running a government inside a diminished constitutional shell. A QUARREL WITH A LONG FUSE It is tempting to read this as a sudden combustion, but the rift has been smouldering for nearly two years. Mehdi joined a student agitation over reservation policy as early as December 2024, after which he says the party leadership effectively stopped speaking to him. Through 2025 he pressed, in public and at party forums, for the National Conference to treat restoration of Articles 370 and 35A as a live commitment rather than a rhetorical inheritance, walking out of a working-committee meeting in May after a sharp exchange with Chief Minister Omar Abdullah. By December he was warning of a sit-in over reservation rationalisation and questioning what he called selective demolitions in Jammu. The party’s defeat in the Budgam Assembly bypoll this year appears to have hardened positions on both sides, removing whatever incentive existed for a patched-up truce. What has changed in August 2026 is not the substance of the disagreement but its openness — Farooq Abdullah’s decision to publicly demand resignation, and Mehdi’s decision to answer with a letter rather than a retreat. THE LETTER AS INDICTMENT, NOT APOLOGY Mehdi’s letter to Abdullah is worth reading closely because it refuses the terms on which such letters are usually written. It does not apologise; it interrogates. He notes that Abdullah’s own press remarks — asking Kashmiris how long they would remain “slaves” and accusing critics of “begging” from Delhi — could as easily describe the NC’s own current posture of settling for statehood. His central claim is that statehood was never meant to be a ceiling, only a floor, and that treating it as the outer horizon of political ambition quietly legitimises the constitutional rupture of August 2019. He is not wrong that the 2024 manifesto committed the party to seeking restoration of Articles 370 and 35A alongside statehood; that promise is on paper, not merely in memory. His sharpest line is also his fairest one: the BJP was in power when the manifesto was written, so the argument that restoration is now impossible cannot explain why the promise was made in the first place. ABDULLAH’S CASE, AND ITS LIMITS Dr. Farooq Abdullah’s public response has been blunter than persuasive. Telling Mehdi that his 2024 victory depended on the party symbol, daring him to resign and “go back to the people,” and advising him to consult the Quran to find the “right path” reads less like an argument about strategy and more like an assertion of patriarchal authority. The invocation of 1984 — a year that still carries the scar tissue of Farooq Abdullah’s own government being toppled by defectors — was presumably meant as a warning, but it also inadvertently reveals how personally the NC president has taken this challenge, sixty years into a political life built on exactly the kind of loyalty he now finds wanting in a man he brought into the party himself. What Abdullah has not offered, and what the moment badly needs, is a reasoned defence of sequencing: why statehood first, why Article 370 later, and on what timeline restoration might still be attempted through Parliament rather than through street politics. His single concession — that Mehdi is “a Parliament member” and free to raise Article 370 there — concedes the legitimacy of the demand while declining to own it as party policy. THE DEEPER PROBLEM IS STRUCTURAL, NOT PERSONAL This is where a measured reading must part from both camps. The National Conference’s 2024 manifesto tried to do two things that Kashmir’s current constitutional position makes very difficult to hold together: promise a maximal restoration of pre-2019 status, and promise workable, negotiated governance within a Union Territory administration that reports substantially to Delhi. Those two commitments can coexist as aspirations. They become unstable the moment a party actually forms a government, because governing requires daily transactions with the same authority whose 2019 actions the manifesto pledged to reverse. Mehdi’s insistence on keeping the maximal demand alive is not merely idealism; it names a real risk, that the passage of time converts an emergency into a routine, and that a population’s disempowerment becomes something to be managed rather than resisted. But Abdullah’s insistence on statehood as the practical, sequenced first step also names something real: that a party without administrative power to protect land, jobs, and local institutions cannot fight for anything at all, however loudly it speaks in opposition. WHAT MEHDI’S EXIT WILL AND WILL NOT SETTLE If Mehdi does resign on 3 November as indicated, the ensuing Srinagar by-election will function as an informal referendum, though an imperfect one, on whether his position commands an independent electoral base or was always borrowed from the National Conference’s organisational strength. Abdullah has bet, publicly and repeatedly, that Mehdi’s 2024 margin of over 350,000 votes belonged to the party symbol, not the man. Mehdi has bet that his own credibility — as the son of a man killed for his politics, and as a rare voice within a ruling party willing to embarrass his own chief minister — will translate into votes cast on principle. Both men are, in effect, gambling with the same electorate’s patience. Whatever the by-election shows, it will not resolve the structural tension that produced this rupture. Even if Mehdi wins as an independent—or loses and recedes from immediate political prominence—the National Conference will still be governing a Union Territory after having promised a wider constitutional restoration that it has yet to deliver. The next MP from Srinagar, whoever it may be, will inherit the same unresolved question Mehdi’s letter has placed before Farooq Abdullah: has the party’s political horizon permanently narrowed to what New Delhi is willing to concede, or does its 2024 promise still carry political meaning? That question will outlast this particular feud and, in all likelihood, the present protagonists. The National Conference’s future will not be decided by a quarrel between personalities, nor by whether Mehdi ultimately returns to its fold. It will be decided by whether the party still believes that its promises are obligations rather than instruments of electoral convenience. If a party that sought votes in the name of constitutional dignity now treats that very promise as a negotiable inconvenience, it may retain the seat of government while losing the confidence that once made it a movement. The real test, therefore, is not only what Mehdi will do next. It is whether the National Conference can recover the moral courage to clarify its course, renew its pledge, and keep faith with those who voted for it. Until it does, the Valley’s political future will remain unsettled—not because dissent has weakened the party, but because the party has yet to answer the dissent that its own promises have produced. Colonel Maqbool Shah is an ex-Indian Army officer. He writes on strategic affairs, culture and mundane issues. While in service, he also served as the UN Liaison Officer across 42 countries with Iraq’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Baghdad after the First Gulf War.

stories.headline: India looks to expand Iran trade amid US curbs
stories.title: India looks to expand Iran trade amid US curbs
stories.summary: New Delhi: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek, in what was their maiden in-person engagement since the war and discussed expanding and diversifying trade ties and reiterated New Delhi's commitment "to strengthening India's long-standing friendship with Iran across diverse sectors"."Met President Masoud Pezeshkian in Bishkek. Reiterated our commitment to strengthening India's long-standing friendship with Iran across diverse sectors. We want to expand and diversify our trade basket in the times to come," Modi wrote on X following his meeting with Pezeshkian. This statement signals India's willingness to widen trade partnership with Iran amid the US sanctions on the Persian Gulf state.During the meeting, Modi also called for freedom of navigation and protecting the lives of seafarers in the backdrop of the challenges faced by India amid the volatility in West Asia. Since the war, Modi and the Iranian President had held three telephone conversations on the Hormuz Strait navigation and the conflict situation.Modi informed Pezeshkian of India's readiness to closely cooperate with Iran in multilateral organisations, including BRICS and SCO, and conveyed that he looked forward to welcoming President Pezeshkian to India for the BRICS summit here on September 12-13, according to an official.It is understood that the two leaders discussed Iran's position on the war that it wants to be reflected in the BRICS declaration and India's views on BRICS unity.The two leaders discussed various aspects of bilateral ties, including Iran's energy exports to India and retaining India's interests in the Chabahar Port through an arrangement with Tehran. They discussed the recent developments in the West Asia conflict and shared perspectives on the evolving situation, according to a readout by the Ministry of External Affairs.

During the meeting, Modi also called for freedom of navigation and protecting the lives of seafarers in the backdrop of the challenges faced by India amid the volatility in West Asia.
Since the war, Modi and the Iranian President had held three telephone conversations on the Hormuz Strait navigation and the conflict situation.

Modi informed Pezeshkian of India's readiness to closely cooperate with Iran in multilateral organisations, including BRICS and SCO, and conveyed that he looked forward to welcoming President Pezeshkian to India for the BRICS summit here on September 12-13, according to an official.
It is understood that the two leaders discussed Iran's position on the war that it wants to be reflected in the BRICS declaration and India's views on BRICS unity.
The two leaders discussed various aspects of bilateral ties, including Iran's energy exports to India and retaining India's interests in the Chabahar Port through an arrangement with Tehran.
They discussed the recent developments in the West Asia conflict and shared perspectives on the evolving situation, according to a readout by the Ministry of External Affairs.

stories.headline: SC Collegium recommends Justice P S Bhati as CJ of J&K, Ladakh HC
stories.title: SC Collegium recommends Justice P S Bhati as CJ of J&K, Ladakh HC
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 31: The Supreme Court Collegium Monday recommended the elevation of Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati of the Rajasthan High Court as Chief Justice of the High Court of J&K and Ladakh. The Collegium, headed by the Chief Justice of India, also recommended Justice Sanjay K Agrawal of the Chhattisgarh High Court for appointment as Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court and Justice Alpesh Yeshvant Kogje of the Gujarat High Court as Chief Justice of the Madhya Pradesh High Court. Born on September 21, 1970, Justice Bhati enrolled as an advocate in 1992 and was elevated to the Rajasthan High Court Bench on November 16, 2016. He holds a BA and LLB, besides an LLM in Mercantile Law and a PhD on 'Promotion and Seniority in Public Employment, its Changing Dimensions and Role of Supreme Court.' Prior to his elevation, Justice Bhati practised mainly at the Rajasthan High Court in Jodhpur, handling matters relating to writ jurisdiction, service laws, public interest litigation, elections, revenue, mining, education, Panchayati Raj, family and criminal law, among others. He served as Additional Advocate General of Rajasthan and was associated with several government departments and public institutions as panel counsel. He was also Standing Counsel for the Indian Railways for 16 years and represented institutions including the Reserve Bank of India and Jai Narain Vyas University.

stories.headline: Bridging the link between science and ground reality
stories.title: Bridging the link between science and ground reality
stories.summary: SHEIKH ANEAUS The latest catastrophe in Nepal serves as a terrible illustration. In order to reconstruct what transpired high in the mountains, scientists are currently analyzing hydrological observations, satellite pictures, and more data. However, the incident happened so fast that community downstream had very little time to react. Experts have since stressed the importance of better satellite monitoring, real-time river monitoring, quicker detection of blockages and stronger early-warning systems to help reduce the impact of such events. The problem is not always a deficiency of scientific data. There are instances when the information is available but the connection between monitoring, research, and action is insufficient. Scientific studies are giving us clearer picture of how the landscape is changing around us. Satellites are tracking glaciers and lakes, field expeditions are carried out to record changes in mountainous regions, weather stations are collecting observations, and researchers are using these observations to better understand natural hazards such as floods and landslides. But collecting information is only one part of the job. The true worth of research is demonstrated when the data aids in decision-making. In areas where infrastructure and people can be rapidly impacted by environmental changes, this becomes particularly crucial. A change seen in a high-altitude lake or glacier could start as a scientific observation. When that information is coupled to the settlements, roads, bridges, power projects, and other facilities that are located downstream, its significance becomes much more evident. That link between research and application needs to remain strong. This does not suggest that government organizations and researchers operate independently. Environmental risks are already being monitored and understood by a number of entities. The Geological Survey of India, the Central Water Commission, the National Disaster Management Authority, ISRO and its National Remote Sensing Center, the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, and other scientific organizations are working on various aspects of mountain hazards, monitoring, and disaster preparedness. Additionally, the Central Water Commission has created a risk-indexing method for glacial lakes, and it is working with organizations like ISRO and C-DAC to build early warning systems. These initiatives offer a critical base. The next step is to assure that the information produced through them can move smoothly between those who generate it and those who need to act on it. A change in a glacier, lake, or mountain slope could be detected by a researcher. An organization in charge of disaster management might need to determine if that change needs to be addressed right now. It may be necessary for a local government to know which routes or settlements might be impacted. The infrastructure department may need to know if a project or bridge is located in a potentially dangerous area. Each of these may only be a part of the picture. Combining those components can provide a much clearer picture of the true danger. This is where regular information exchange becomes important. Researchers require access to relevant ground data, while implementing agencies want timely access to scientific findings. Similarly, in-situ observations can also help researchers understand changes that might not be apparent from satellite imagery alone. For instance, a satellite image indicates that a lake has expanded. That information becomes much more useful when it is combined with the condition of the surrounding slopes, the drainage of the lake and the location of settlements and infrastructure in downstream areas. This also holds true for other hazards. When a rainfall forecast is combined with the data pertaining to slopes prone to landslides, it becomes more valuable. When highways, bridges, and settlements are included, in a flood map it is much more helpful. Glacier change when connected with information on the drainage system beneath it, is a value addition. In many cases, the information is already available, but bringing it all together is the challenge. This doesn't always mean that new systems need to be developed. When data from many sources is combined and updated on a regular basis, monitoring programs, databases, and communication channels can become more beneficial. The important question is how effectively these different sources of information can work together when a situation develops. An official might want a far more straightforward response, even though a research report might include a thorough scientific analysis: Is there a change? Where's it? What might take place? Which regions are at risk? What should I watch after this? That does not imply eliminating uncertainty or reducing the science to a few numbers. It is quite the reverse. Making wise choices requires an awareness of both the known and the unknown. Closer observation or a ground monitoring may be the best course of action if the information at hand is insufficient to assess if a change is hazardous. It could be necessary to do additional modeling if a potential flood pathway is unclear. Authorities don't need to wait for all the answers to scientific questions to start planning if a vulnerable location is already known. This strategy can assist prevent unwarranted worry and complacency. Scientific data on glaciers, rainfall, rivers, terrain and past disasters can be combined with information on settlements and infrastructure to identify areas where environmental hazards may affect people. This can help guide infrastructure planning, evacuation routes and field monitoring, making research part of regular planning rather than a response after disasters. Local communities can also provide useful information, as they often notice changes in water levels, slopes, cracks and streams before they are recorded officially. This kind of observation cannot replace scientific monitoring, but they can add another layer of information. This also applies to early warning systems. Instrument installation is crucial, but an alert is only helpful if someone understands what it signifies and what needs to be done. Communities need to know exactly where to go, which routes to take, and how fast they might need to react. Therefore, preparation must start long in advance of an emergency. Identifying susceptible areas, comprehending potential risks, inspecting vital infrastructure, enhancing communication routes, and determining ahead of time who is in charge of what should all be part of it. This process can be greatly facilitated by stronger relationships between researchers and implementing authorities. Researchers can help identify emerging risks and explain what the available evidence means. Government departments can identify the information they need for planning and response. Local authorities and communities can provide information from the ground level. It should work both ways. Additionally, it should occur on a regular basis rather than just in the immediate aftermath of a calamity. A risk assessment completed a few years ago might not accurately reflect current conditions since environmental variables vary over time. Thus, frequent updates are just as crucial as the original evaluation. Creating more meetings or paperwork shouldn't be the goal. It ought to be to better utilize the data that is already being produced. Examples of research being beneficial outside of academia include a satellite image that prompts a field inspection, a field observation that enhances a risk map, a hazard map that modifies an infrastructure design, or an early warning that allows people enough time to evacuate to safety. We have the chance to accomplish this more successfully than in the past thanks to the expanding availability of satellite data, enhanced computation, better monitoring systems, and field observations. However, technology by itself won't bridge the divide. A habit of exchanging knowledge, posing pertinent questions, and maintaining open lines of communication between those who research a hazard and those who must prepare for it is what are required. Environmental risks can't always be avoided, and it's not always possible to foresee when they will occur. However, when information is accessible early and handled appropriately, their effects are frequently reduced. The goal should not simply be to produce more research. It should be to make the research we already have easier to share, understand and use. For downstream communities, the value of this work is quite simple. It means knowing when something has changed above them, understanding whether they may be at risk, and receiving a warning early enough to move themselves and their families to safety. Monitoring cannot prevent every flood, landslide or other mountain hazard. But timely information can give people something very important - time. Time to leave, time to close a road, time to move equipment, time to warn others and, most importantly, time to save lives. That is why bringing research and implementation closer together matters. It is not only about understanding how the landscape is changing. It is about making sure that what we learn reaches the people at the helm before the hazard reaches them. (The Author is a PhD in Geoinformatics. Feedback: sheikh.aneaus19@gmail.com)

stories.headline: After Supreme Court judge’s letters, Collegium recommends new Chief Justice for Rajasthan HC
stories.title: After Supreme Court judge’s letters, Collegium recommends new Chief Justice for Rajasthan HC
stories.summary: Resolution by the Collegium came a weekend after letters written by serving top court judge Justice Sandeep Mehta, complaining of the conduct of Rajasthan Acting Chief Justice S.P. Sharma, became public
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'chief justice' in title weight 42
event term: 'chief justice' in summary weight 25.2
article_sentences: The Supreme Court Collegium on Monday (August 31, 2026) recommended Chhattisgarh High Court judge, Justice Sanjay K. Agrawal, for appointment as the Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court.

The resolution by the Collegium headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant came days after letters written by serving top court judge Justice Sandeep Mehta, complaining of the conduct of Rajasthan Acting Chief Justice S.P. Sharma, became public.
Justice Mehta, in a series of three letters in August, had accused Justice Sharma of “favouritism” and misconduct.
The Supreme Court judge highlighted that his entreaties to Chief Justice Kant to transfer Justice Sharma out of Rajasthan failed to evoke any response.
Justice Mehta had sought a regular Chief Justice for the Rajasthan High Court.
Justice Sharma had been the Acting Chief Justice for the past 10 months.
Chief Justice Kant had issued a press statement the same day the letters came into the public domain.
In his statement, the CJI had said the Collegium would consider Justice Mehta’s allegations through an institutional mechanism.
The Collegium has also recommended new Chief Justices for two other High Courts – Madhya Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

Justices Alpesh Yeshvant Kogje of Gujarat and Dr. Pushpinder Singh Bhati of Rajasthan have been suggested for appointment as Chief Justices of Madhya Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Courts, respectively.

In a separate resolution, the Supreme Court Collegium said it had recommended, in a meeting held on August 6, to appoint Justice Krushna Ram Mohapatra, a judge of the High Court of Orissa, as Chief Justice of the Chhattisgarh High Court on the retirement of the incumbent on September 4, 2026.
The Collegium has, in a separate resolution, recommended the immediate transfer of Justice Agrawal to the Rajasthan High Court, pending his appointment as its Chief Justice.

stories.headline: Nitish Kumar takes charge as ADGP Armed Police J&K
stories.title: Nitish Kumar takes charge as ADGP Armed Police J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 31: Senior IPS officer Nitish Kumar on Monday took charge as the Additional Director General of Police (ADGP), Armed Police, following the recent Home Department reshuffle. Kumar, a 1999-batch AGMUT cadre officer, was accorded a guard of honour on his arrival at the Armed Police Headquarters here. He subsequently interacted with senior officers and was briefed on the functioning, deployment and operational responsibilities of the Armed Police wing. Kumar was transferred from the post of ADGP, CID, J&K, in a major reshuffle ordered by the Home Department on August 27 through Government Order No 438-Home of 2026. He had also been holding the additional charge of Director, State Investigation Agency (SIA). As part of the reshuffle, 1996-batch IPS officer M K Sinha was posted as ADGP, CID, J&K, replacing Kumar. The latest assignment places Kumar at the helm of the Armed Police wing at a time when the force continues to play a key role in maintaining security and law and order across J&K, besides providing manpower for operational, protective and other security-related duties. During his initial interaction with senior officers, he was briefed about the functioning of the Armed Police, its various formations, deployments and other operational matters. He is expected to review the existing arrangements and priorities of the force in the coming days. The ADGP has extensive experience in policing, counter-terrorism, intelligence, and investigations in J&K. An engineering graduate, he joined the Indian Police Service in 2000 and belongs to the 1999 AGMUT cadre. His earlier field assignments in J&K include SSP Handwara, SSP Pulwama, and SSP Anantnag. He subsequently served as DIG, South Kashmir Range, Anantnag, and DIG, North Kashmir Range, Baramulla, gaining extensive operational experience in some of the most security-sensitive areas of J&K. Kumar was posted as IGP, CID, J&K, in March 2023 following his repatriation from central deputation, during which he served with the National Investigation Agency (NIA) and the Cabinet Secretariat. He was promoted to the rank of ADGP in February 2024 while continuing with the CID. In March 2024, he was also given additional charge as Director of the SIA, which handles several sensitive investigations related to terrorism and other security-linked cases. Before his central deputation, Kumar had also served as IGP, Technical Services, J&K Police. His service record includes several decorations for distinguished policing. He was awarded the Police Medal for Gallantry in 2007 and 2008, the Police Medal for Meritorious Service in 2015, and the President’s Police Medal for Distinguished Service in 2025.

stories.headline: Met predicts isolated spell of heavy rains in Jammu division for 2 days
stories.title: Met predicts isolated spell of heavy rains in Jammu division for 2 days
stories.summary: Amid persisting orange alert across Jammu for two days, the weather department has predicted isolated heavy rains with thunder storms, lightning and gusty winds for the entire Jammu region, with the possibilities of landslides, shooting stones and flash floods at vulnerable places on September 1 and 2. During the next 24 hours, as per weatherman, there will be isolated heavy falls in Jammu division while there will be fairly widespread light to moderate rain coupled with thunderstorms in the subsequent two days. As per India Meteorological Department (IMD) Centre, parts of the division may witness spells of showers with gusty winds during late night on Monday, August 31. “In Jammu division, during the intervening nights of August 31-September 1 and September 1 and 2, there is possibility of heavy spell particularly in Jammu, Kathua districts and adjoining areas. Rajouri-Poonch areas too may witness a spell or two of isolated moderate to heavy showers during next 24 to 48 hours,” the weatherman predicted. “There are chances of heavy showers in Jammu division with the possibility of mudslides, landslides and flash floods at higher and vulnerable places. After September 2, there will be improvement in the weather. Till September 10, there are no chances of major events,” the Met department has anticipated. The weather conditions would continue to be hot and humid amid scattered spells. The maximum temperature in Jammu is likely to swing between 31 to 33 degrees Celsius, amid hot and humid weather conditions. After September 15, according to the weatherman, the temperature is likely to witness a significant fall.
